lessons.title: From source to running program
lessons.objective: Explain the separate compile and run steps of a minimal C program.
explanation: A source file is readable program text, conventionally named with a .c suffix. A compiler translates it and checks its syntax. Linking joins compiled code with library code to produce an executable. Running starts that executable; changing source does not change an older executable until you build again.

This course compiles as C17 explicitly, with gcc -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic main.c -o program, then runs ./program. C17 is a deliberate stable baseline, not the newest C standard. The application performs these separate operations for you and reports failures from each stage.

#include <stdio.h> makes standard input/output declarations available, including printf. int main(void) is the program entry point: int says it returns an integer status, and void says it accepts no parameters here. Braces contain its statements. printf displays the quoted text; return 0 reports successful completion.
walkthrough: The include line gives the compiler the declaration needed to use printf correctly; it does not print anything.
Execution begins in main. The printf call displays Hello, C! followed by a newline.
The semicolon ends the call statement. return 0 ends main with a success status; the status is separate from printed output.

prediction.question: Does compiling this file by itself display Hello, C!?
prediction.answer: No. Running the resulting executable displays it.
prediction.explanation: Compilation creates the program. printf runs only during execution.

lessons.recap: Source → compile/link → executable → run. A build failure and a program failure are different events.

retrieval.question: What does return 0 communicate to the program that launched this executable?
retrieval.answer: Successful completion; it is not text printed to the screen.

lessons.title: Put text on separate lines
lessons.objective: Use newline and quote escapes to format a small text report.
explanation: printf means formatted print. For now, give it one string literal: text enclosed in double quotes. A literal is a value written directly into the source. The surrounding quotes delimit the text and are not part of the output.

A backslash begins an escape sequence inside a string. \n represents a newline, \" represents a double quote, and \\ represents one backslash. These source spellings each describe a character; printf does not display their backslashes literally unless you escape the backslash.

Two calls execute in source order. A newline moves the following text to a new line. Without it, calls can appear together on one line. Output is a byte stream, so the app preserves line breaks and spaces instead of silently inventing a layout.
walkthrough: The first call writes the title and ends its line with \n.
The \" escapes let the second string contain visible double quotes without ending the literal.
Both statements finish with semicolons. main returns after both calls have executed.

prediction.question: How many output lines appear, and are the quote characters visible?
prediction.answer: Two lines; the second is Say "hello".
prediction.explanation: Each \n ends a line. Escaped quotes are characters inside the string.

lessons.recap: Escapes describe characters inside quoted text; statement order determines output order.

retrieval.question: What source escape produces one visible backslash?
retrieval.answer: \\ inside a string literal.

lessons.title: Statements, comments, and useful diagnostics
lessons.objective: Distinguish executable statements from comments and repair a compiler-reported source error.
explanation: A statement asks the program to do something, such as calling printf or returning a status. A block is the group inside braces. Whitespace and indentation make a block readable, but semicolons and braces define its syntax.

// starts a comment that ends at the next newline. /* and */ delimit a block comment. Comments explain intent and are ignored during translation; they do not print. Block comments cannot be nested. Prefer a short reason over a comment that merely repeats the code.

The compiler reports errors when it cannot build the program, and warnings when it notices suspicious code. Read the first message first, with its filename and line number. A missing character can make the next line look wrong, so inspect the nearby source too. This course keeps warnings visible; a successful build is still worth checking.
walkthrough: The // comment stops at its newline. It does not become output.
The printf statement is executable and prints the status label.
The block comment documents return 0 below it. Comments cannot replace a needed semicolon.

prediction.question: Will either comment appear in stdout?
prediction.explanation: Comments are removed during translation, before the program executes.

lessons.recap: Use comments for intent. Use compiler locations as clues and fix the first relevant error.

retrieval.question: Can a /* block comment contain another nested /* ... */ block comment?
retrieval.answer: No. The first closing */ ends the comment.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: a readable first program
lessons.objective: Build and explain a small report without copying a malformed template.
explanation: Bring the pieces together: include the declaration for printf, use int main(void), place statements in a braced block, and return a status. A program can compile successfully and still print the wrong text, so check both the build result and the output.

A useful small check compares the intended lines with actual stdout. This checkpoint asks for exact labels, punctuation, and line breaks because those are the behavior being learned. It does not require a particular number of printf calls or enforce one formatting style.

Before running, predict each line in order. If compilation fails, inspect the first diagnostic. If output differs, inspect the literals and escapes. A warning-free build and a passing check are evidence for these tested cases, not proof that every possible program is correct.
walkthrough: The report has three lines because each string ends in a newline.
The text C17 is a label. The actual language choice comes from the compiler flag, not from this string.
return 0 reports success independently of all three printed lines.

prediction.question: If you change the text C17 to C23 without changing compiler flags, does the dialect change?
prediction.answer: No. The build still selects C17.
prediction.explanation: Printed labels do not configure the compiler; -std=c17 does.

lessons.recap: A working program needs both valid syntax and behavior that matches its goal.

retrieval.question: Name one difference between a compiler diagnostic and stdout.
retrieval.answer: A diagnostic describes a build issue; stdout is text produced by running the program.

lessons.title: Variables, initialization, and types
lessons.objective: Initialize named values and choose basic types for quantities.
explanation: A variable names an object that stores a value. A declaration gives it a type, such as int for ordinary integers or double for floating-point quantities. An initializer supplies its first value: int sessions = 3;. Read a local variable only after giving it a value.

A literal writes a value directly: 3 is an integer literal, 1.5 is a floating-point literal, and 'A' is a character constant. A char object holds a character-sized integer value. C does not promise that int has exactly 32 bits; choose representable values and do not expect signed overflow to wrap.

An assignment replaces a stored value, as in sessions = 4;. const double minutes = 7.5; says this object must not be modified through that name. printf placeholders connect types to text: %d for int, %f for double, and %c for a character promoted to int. The corresponding arguments follow the format string in order.
walkthrough: All three objects are initialized before use. const makes minutes a value this code does not assign again.
The assignment changes sessions from 3 to 4. It does not print anything itself.
%d prints the int; %.1f prints the double with one digit after the decimal point; %c prints the character.

prediction.question: What does the Sessions line contain: 3 or 4?
prediction.explanation: The assignment runs before printf and replaces the initial value.

lessons.recap: Initialize before reading, choose a suitable type, and match printf placeholders to arguments.

retrieval.question: What is the difference between int n = 3; and n = 4;?
retrieval.answer: The first declares and initializes n; the second assigns a new value to an already declared object.

lessons.title: Arithmetic and deliberate conversion
lessons.objective: Distinguish integer division from floating-point division and control evaluation order.
explanation: Expressions combine values with operators. * / and % bind more tightly than + and -, so 2 + 3 * 4 is 14. Parentheses make a chosen order explicit. % is the integer remainder operator. Keep examples within their types' representable ranges: signed overflow has undefined behavior.

When both operands of / are integers, division produces an integer quotient and discards the fractional part toward zero. Assigning that result to double afterward cannot recover the lost fraction. 7 / 2 is 3, while 7.0 / 2 is 3.5 because one operand is floating-point.

A cast explicitly requests a conversion, such as (double)total. For small int values here that conversion is exact. Convert before the division when a fractional result is needed. Conversion from a representable floating-point value to int discards its fractional part; it is not rounding. Never divide by zero.
walkthrough: Integer division yields 3, and the remainder is 1.
The cast changes the left operand before division, so mean receives 3.5.
Multiplication happens first in the ungrouped expression; the parentheses change the grouped result to 20.

prediction.question: Would double mean = total / count; give 3.5?
prediction.explanation: The int division happens first. Only its already-truncated result is converted during assignment.

lessons.recap: Choose operand types before division, and use parentheses to express intended grouping.

retrieval.question: How can 9 and 4 produce a fractional quotient without changing their int declarations?
retrieval.answer: Use (double)9 / 4, or cast the named left operand before division.

lessons.title: Format values and inspect type sizes
lessons.objective: Match printf argument types and use sizeof without assuming fixed type widths.
explanation: A format string is a small instruction language for printf. %d expects an int, %u an unsigned int, %ld a long, %f a double, and %zu the size_t value produced by sizeof. %% prints a literal percent sign and consumes no argument. A mismatched variadic argument type can cause undefined behavior; compiler warnings help find it.

sizeof reports an object or type's size in C bytes. A C byte is the unit occupied by char, so sizeof(char) is always 1; a byte need not contain exactly eight bits on every C implementation. Other type sizes depend on the implementation. Do not make a lesson check expect int to be four bytes.

unsigned int stores nonnegative integers; it is not a universal fix for arithmetic mistakes. long may have a wider range than int, but its size still varies. %zu matters even if size_t happens to have the same width as another type. %.2f controls displayed fractional digits, not the stored precision.
walkthrough: The u and L suffixes make the literals unsigned int and long respectively; each format matches its argument.
%% prints one visible percent sign. %.2f prints two digits after the decimal point.
sizeof(char) is 1 by definition. sizeof(int) is reported honestly for this toolchain rather than assumed portable.

prediction.question: Which output size is guaranteed here: sizeof(char) or sizeof(int)?
prediction.explanation: C defines one byte as the size of char. The int size is implementation-dependent.

lessons.recap: Printf formats describe argument types. sizeof results use %zu and do not establish universal type widths.

retrieval.question: Which printf conversion prints the result of sizeof?
retrieval.answer: %zu, because sizeof produces size_t.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: a numerical utility
lessons.objective: Calculate a bounded numerical report with correct conversions and formatting.
explanation: This utility uses provided data, so it does not need input parsing yet. Give each quantity a name and type, then decide which operations should remain integer and which should produce fractions. Do not assume that assigning to double changes the arithmetic that came before it.

Integer quotient and remainder describe equal whole groups. A mean is usually fractional. Keep the data small enough for the chosen types, and explicitly avoid zero divisors. In later modules, you will validate external values before calculating.

A numerical check covers both result and presentation. Predict each expression, then compare the report. If a result is wrong, trace operand values and types before changing the format: printing more decimal places cannot repair a truncated integer division.
walkthrough: const marks the supplied data as unchanged within the calculation.
The integer calculation yields 4 whole items per day and 3 spare items.
The cast selects floating-point division, yielding 4.75 instead of the integer quotient 4.

prediction.question: What is lost if you write (double)(total / days)?
prediction.answer: The fractional part is already lost; the result is 4.0.
prediction.explanation: The parentheses evaluate integer division before the cast.

lessons.recap: Trace values and operand types together when checking arithmetic.

retrieval.question: How can a program correctly display four whole groups and a mean of 4.75 from the same data?
retrieval.answer: Use integer division for whole groups and floating-point division for the mean.

lessons.title: Comparisons and truth values
lessons.objective: Build conditions with comparisons and distinguish equality from assignment.
explanation: A comparison answers a yes/no question. < <= > >= compare order, == compares equality, and != compares inequality. Each result has type int and value 1 for true or 0 for false. A condition treats zero as false and any nonzero value as true.

The logical operators &&, ||, and ! mean and, or, and not. They also produce 0 or 1. Parenthesize comparisons when combining them to make the rule readable. A range check is (score >= 0) && (score <= 100), not 0 <= score <= 100; C does not interpret the latter as mathematical chaining.

= assigns a value; == asks whether two values are equal. An assignment expression also has a value, so using it accidentally in a condition can compile and change your data. Warnings help, but carefully reading the intended question remains necessary.
walkthrough: Both range comparisons are true, so valid receives 1.
score == 70 tests equality and leaves score unchanged; exact receives 0.
!0 produces 1 because zero is false. Logical results are normalized to 0 or 1.

prediction.question: What values do valid and exact hold?
prediction.explanation: 72 is in the inclusive range but is not equal to 70.

lessons.recap: Conditions test values; = changes a value and == compares it.

retrieval.question: Why is 0 <= score <= 100 not a correct C range test?
retrieval.answer: C evaluates the first comparison to 0 or 1, then compares that result with 100. Use two comparisons joined by &&.

lessons.title: Choose a branch with if and else
lessons.objective: Implement ordered if/else rules and test their boundary values.
explanation: if (condition) executes its following statement when the condition is true. else supplies an alternative when it is false. Use braces around branch blocks even when they contain one statement: adding a second statement later then remains clear.

An else if chain tests conditions in order and takes the first matching branch. Put a narrow or higher-priority rule before a broader overlapping rule. The last else handles all remaining cases. Conditions should make the intended boundary inclusive or exclusive explicitly.

A useful check includes values just below a boundary, exactly at it, and just above it. For a rule that starts at 60, test 59, 60, and 61. We use provided data here; validated keyboard input comes later after strings and pointers.
walkthrough: 60 does not satisfy score >= 80, so execution continues to the next condition.
60 does satisfy score >= 60, including the boundary, so Pass is printed.
Only one branch runs. The higher threshold is checked before the lower overlapping one.

prediction.question: What happens for score 80 if the >= 60 branch is checked first?
prediction.answer: It matches that earlier branch, so a later distinction branch is skipped.
prediction.explanation: An else if chain stops at the first true condition.

lessons.recap: Order overlapping rules deliberately and test values around every threshold.

retrieval.question: Which three values are a useful first boundary test for score >= 60?

lessons.title: Short-circuit guards and switch cases
lessons.objective: Use evaluation order to guard division and handle a small discrete choice.
explanation: && evaluates its left operand first and skips the right operand when the left is false. || skips the right operand when the left is true. This is short-circuit evaluation. A guard such as count != 0 && total / count > 3 checks that division is possible before evaluating it.

Order matters in a guard. Reversing those operands could divide by zero before checking count. Avoid hiding necessary work inside a condition: the skipped operand will not run. Read the condition as an ordered calculation, not just a truth table.

switch selects a case by an integer or enumeration value; here we use an int. case labels are distinct integer constant expressions, and default handles unmatched values. After a match, execution continues until break or another control transfer. Use break to avoid accidental fallthrough when each choice should act separately.
walkthrough: count != 0 is false, so total / count is not evaluated; there is no division by zero.
The if takes its else block. This reports that there is no valid large mean, rather than calculating an invalid one.
mode 2 selects case 2. break exits the switch before default can execute.

prediction.question: Does the worked example evaluate total / count when count is zero?
prediction.answer: No. && short-circuits after the false guard.
prediction.explanation: The safety test is the left operand and is evaluated first.

lessons.recap: Place safety checks first in short-circuit conditions; end separate switch choices with break.

retrieval.question: What does break do inside a switch?
retrieval.answer: It exits that switch, preventing unintended continuation into later case bodies.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: a branching rule
lessons.objective: Combine validity checks and ordered classifications without changing the data.
explanation: A classification rule has two different concerns: whether the data is in its allowed range and which category it belongs to. Check validity before assigning a category. This avoids describing an impossible score as an excellent result.

Keep equality tests separate from assignments, include deliberate boundary choices, and use braces. For inclusive 0–100 scores, values -1 and 101 are invalid; values 0 and 100 are valid. For a passing threshold of 60, 59 fails and 60 passes.

The exercise data is fixed, so a passing behavior check covers that case. You can use Run to probe other constants. Later, function-level tests will call the same rule across many inputs. Until then, do not mistake one successful printed classification for complete proof of the rule.
walkthrough: The first branch rejects values outside the inclusive 0–100 range.
101 is invalid even though it also exceeds the distinction threshold.
Only valid values reach the ordered category rules. The final else includes all remaining valid scores.

prediction.question: Why must validation come before the distinction branch for score 101?
prediction.answer: Otherwise 101 could be misclassified as Distinction.
prediction.explanation: The category threshold alone does not express the allowed input range.

lessons.recap: Validate the domain, then classify its meaningful values and test the boundaries.

retrieval.question: Give two invalid scores and two valid boundary scores for an inclusive 0–100 domain.
retrieval.answer: Invalid: -1 and 101. Valid boundaries: 0 and 100.

lessons.title: While loops and progress
lessons.objective: Trace a bounded while loop and identify how it terminates.
explanation: A loop repeats a block. while checks its condition before every iteration, including the first. An iteration is one execution of the body. If the condition begins false, the body runs zero times. A counter records which iteration is next.

For a bounded counter loop, establish a starting value, test a bound, and update toward that bound. i = i + 1 increases i by one; i++ is a shorter increment form we will use in for loops. Forgetting an update can make the loop run forever. The runner has a deadline, but a deadline is a safety limit, not a correct termination strategy.

An invariant is a fact that stays true at a chosen point on each iteration. Here, before each condition test, i names the next integer to print and stays between 1 and 4. Tracing a few iterations connects the invariant to the stopping rule. The visualizer is a curated teaching simulation, not a live trace of arbitrary source.
walkthrough: i begins at 1, which satisfies i <= 3. The loop prints 1 then changes i to 2.
The next iterations print 2 and 3. Each update makes progress toward the bound.
After printing 3, i becomes 4. The condition is false, and the final statement prints Next: 4.

prediction.question: How many times does the loop body run, and what is i after it finishes?
prediction.explanation: The condition accepts 1, 2, and 3, then rejects 4 after the final update.

lessons.recap: A bounded while loop needs initialization, a test, and progress toward a stopping condition.

retrieval.question: What happens to a while body if its condition is false on the first test?
retrieval.answer: It runs zero times.

lessons.title: For loops and off-by-one boundaries
lessons.objective: Read the three parts of a for loop and choose an inclusive or exclusive bound.
explanation: A for loop puts initialization, condition, and update in one header: for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++). Initialization runs once. The condition runs before each body execution. The update runs after each completed body, before the next condition test.

The counter declared in this header is scoped to the loop: its name is available in the header and body, not after the loop. ++ adds one; -- subtracts one. Use these updates as separate statements or header updates here, rather than mixing them into expressions where evaluation order is harder to read.

An off-by-one error repeats one time too many or too few. Starting at 0 with i < count gives count iterations when count is a small nonnegative integer. Starting at 1 with i <= count also gives count iterations. Match the starting point to the bound rather than mechanically changing < into <=.
walkthrough: The first loop tests and prints 0, 1, and 2; its upper boundary 3 is excluded.
The second loop prints the human-friendly labels 1, 2, and 3 with an inclusive boundary.
Each loop executes three times. Header variables belong to their individual loops.

prediction.question: How many iterations would for (int i = 0; i <= 3; i++) perform?
prediction.explanation: An inclusive upper bound includes an extra value when counting from zero.

lessons.recap: Read start, test, body, update in order; count the accepted values to check boundaries.

retrieval.question: What values does i take in the body of for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++)?

lessons.title: Accumulate, skip, and stop
lessons.objective: Maintain a running total and distinguish continue from break.
explanation: An accumulator stores a combined result across iterations. Initialize a sum to 0 before adding values; otherwise its earlier contents are not a valid starting point. A counter and an accumulator have different jobs: one selects the next iteration, while the other summarizes work done so far.

continue skips the rest of the current iteration. In a for loop, it proceeds to the header update and then the next condition test. break exits the nearest enclosing loop or switch immediately. Keep updates in mind: continue in a while loop can skip an update placed later in its body.

do { ... } while (condition); tests after the body, so it runs at least once, even when the initial condition is false. Notice its final semicolon. Use it when one initial action is required; do not substitute it for a while loop whose zero-iteration case matters.
walkthrough: The sum starts at zero. Values 1 and 2 contribute normally.
continue skips 3; 4 and 5 contribute; break at 6 ends the loop before adding it. The sum is 12.
The do/while increments trials once before its false condition is checked, so Trials is 1.

prediction.question: Which values reach sum = sum + n, and what is the sum?
prediction.answer: 1, 2, 4, and 5 reach it; the sum is 12.
prediction.explanation: continue skips 3 and break stops before 6 can contribute.

lessons.recap: Initialize accumulators. continue skips an iteration remainder; break exits; do/while tests afterward.

retrieval.question: In a for loop, does continue skip the header update?
retrieval.answer: No. It proceeds to the update, then tests the condition again.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: a bounded statistics task
lessons.objective: Compute a count, total, and mean from generated values without off-by-one or initialization errors.
explanation: A small statistics task combines a loop, a counter, a sum, and a mean. We generate the dataset as integers 1 through 5 because arrays have not been taught yet. That keeps attention on loop behavior and avoids unexplained storage or input code.

The loop invariant describes work already done: before the next iteration, count records how many earlier values were included, and total is their sum. Initialize both to zero. After every included value, update both consistently. Keep this bounded example within the representable int range.

Calculate a mean only when count is nonzero, and convert before division. Check not just the final average but also count and total: two mistakes can occasionally cancel in one summary. These checks expose different parts of the calculation.
walkthrough: The inclusive 1–5 loop has five iterations. Each adds its current value and increments count.
The accumulator contains 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 15, while count is 5.
The guard protects the division for an empty dataset, and the cast gives a floating-point mean of 3.00.

prediction.question: If the condition becomes value < 5, which summaries change?
prediction.answer: Count becomes 4, total becomes 10, and mean becomes 2.50.
prediction.explanation: Only 1 through 4 are included, so all three summaries reflect the missing last value.

lessons.recap: Check the loop boundary, each accumulator, and the conversion before mean division.

retrieval.question: Why check count before calculating total / count?
retrieval.answer: An empty dataset has count zero, and division by zero is invalid.

lessons.title: Give a function a job
lessons.objective: Define a function with parameters and a return value.
explanation: A function packages one small operation under a name. A parameter is a local variable initialized from an argument at each call. In double add_tax(double price), price is the parameter; add_tax(20.0) supplies the argument 20.0.

The return type tells the caller what kind of value comes back. A return statement supplies that value and ends the call. Keep calculation separate from printing so another function can reuse and test the calculation.

A function must be declared before a call. Here its definition appears above main, so that definition also declares its name and types. C17 needs the parameter types; use (void) when a function takes no arguments.
walkthrough: double add_tax(double price) states both the result type and the parameter type.
Calling add_tax(20.0) initializes its local price to 20.0.
return sends 22.0 to main; main stores it and prints two decimal places.

prediction.question: What does this program print?
prediction.explanation: 20.0 × 1.10 gives 22.0; %.2f formats two digits after the decimal point.

lessons.recap: Parameters receive arguments; return sends a result back.

retrieval.question: Why keep printf outside a calculation function?
retrieval.answer: The calculation can be reused and tested without depending on its output format.

lessons.title: Declare first, define once
lessons.objective: Use prototypes and local scope to organize functions.
explanation: A prototype declares a function name, result type, and parameter types without giving its body. int square(int value); lets main call square before its definition. The semicolon ends a declaration; a definition supplies braces and executable statements.

A local variable belongs to the block where it is declared. A variable named result in square is separate from a variable named result in main. Scope is where a name can be used; a caller cannot refer directly to a function’s local names.

Keep the prototype and definition consistent. A compiler diagnostic about conflicting types usually means the declarations disagree. Organize a single file with includes, prototypes, main, and function definitions; multiple files come later.
walkthrough: The prototype announces square before main calls it.
The result inside square is initialized to 16 and returned.
The separately scoped result in main stays 7.

prediction.question: Does square change main’s result? What is printed?
prediction.explanation: Each result name belongs to a different function block.

lessons.recap: A prototype describes a call; a definition implements it. Local names remain local.

retrieval.question: What does a conflicting-types diagnostic suggest?
retrieval.answer: The prototype, definition, or another declaration disagrees about a function’s types.

lessons.title: Copies and local lifetime
lessons.objective: Explain pass-by-value and the lifetime of a local object.
explanation: C passes ordinary arguments by value: a parameter receives a copy. Assigning a new value to that parameter does not change the caller’s variable. To update an ordinary caller variable now, return the new value and assign the result in the caller.

Scope and lifetime answer different questions. Scope determines where a name is visible. Lifetime determines when its object exists. An ordinary automatic local object is created when its block is entered and ceases to exist when the block exits.

The returned integer value survives the call as a value; the local object that held it does not. Later pointer lessons show why retaining an address of an expired local object is unsafe. For now, use parameters and explicit return values to move information between calls.
walkthrough: increment receives its own local copy of count.
The first return value initializes next; count is still 4.
The assignment count = increment(count) explicitly stores the new value in count.

prediction.question: What are the two output lines?
prediction.explanation: Changing the parameter changes its copy; assigning the returned value changes the caller’s variable.

lessons.recap: Use returned values to communicate updates; automatic locals end with their block.

retrieval.question: How are scope and lifetime different?
retrieval.answer: Scope concerns name visibility; lifetime concerns when an object exists.

lessons.title: Build a numerical toolkit
lessons.objective: Combine testable functions and trace a bounded recursive call.
explanation: Use a function boundary when an operation has a clear input and result. A toolkit might separate a sum, a mean, and a classification. Small behavioral tests can check each function independently before the whole program is assembled.

Recursion means a function calls itself. It is optional here and comes after ordinary calls. Every recursive path needs a base case that stops and a step that moves toward it. factorial(3) asks for factorial(2), then factorial(1), then factorial(0); each unfinished call keeps its own parameter.

Recursion consumes finite implementation resources. A loop is often simpler for counting; do not recurse on unbounded input. The following example deliberately accepts only n from 0 to 6, so its unsigned result and small call depth are safe. The project uses fixed provided values; interactive input comes after validation lessons.
walkthrough: factorial(0) returns 1 without making another call.
factorial(3) returns 3 × 2 × 1 × 1; each call has its own n.
Converting a before addition makes the sum floating-point; dividing by 3.0 preserves fractional means.

prediction.question: What would happen if factorial had no stopping condition?
prediction.answer: Calls would continue until resources were exhausted; no successful result is guaranteed.
prediction.explanation: The base case terminates this bounded recursive chain.

lessons.recap: Test functions alone, then compose them. Recursion needs a base case and bounded depth.

retrieval.question: Why is a loop usually preferable for an unbounded counting task?
retrieval.answer: It avoids a call per iteration and makes a simple finite bound easier to inspect.

lessons.title: Keep every index inside the array
lessons.objective: Process a fixed-length array using a valid index bound.
explanation: An array is one object containing a fixed number of adjacent elements of the same type. int scores[3] creates three int elements with indices 0, 1, and 2. Index 3 is outside the array; it is not a fourth element.

At the array’s declaration, sizeof scores / sizeof scores[0] gives its element count. sizeof produces size_t, an unsigned integer type printed with %zu. Use index < count, rather than index <= count, to keep a loop within the array.

A function parameter written const int values[] receives access to the caller’s elements and needs a separate count. It does not receive a complete array copy. This is a parameter convention we will unpack in the pointer module; do not use sizeof values inside that function to discover the array length.
walkthrough: The declaration contains three elements; count is 3.
The loop visits indices 0, 1, and 2 because the comparison is strictly less than count.
The three values add to 13; the boundary at index 3 must not be read.

prediction.question: Is scores[count] a valid element?
prediction.answer: No. The last valid index is count - 1 when count is nonzero.
prediction.explanation: count is the number of elements, not the last element’s index.

lessons.recap: Array length and valid indices are different quantities; pass the length to functions.

retrieval.question: Why is sizeof not an array-length operation on an array parameter?
retrieval.answer: That parameter receives pointer access to elements rather than a complete array object; its sizeof is the pointer size.

lessons.title: Text ends at NUL
lessons.objective: Distinguish character-array capacity from string length.
explanation: A C string is a sequence of characters followed by a NUL character, written \0. This is a zero-valued character, not the printed digit 0. char word[] = "cat" creates four elements: c, a, t, and the terminator.

Capacity is how many elements an array can hold. String length counts characters before the first NUL and excludes the terminator. A char array is not automatically a valid string: if no NUL exists within its readable bounds, passing it to strlen or printf("%s", ...) can read outside the object.

strlen, declared by <string.h>, returns a size_t length and requires an already valid NUL-terminated string. Character literals use single quotes; string literals use double quotes. We will work with byte-based ASCII examples here; counting bytes is not the same as counting all human-language characters.
walkthrough: The initializer includes a terminating NUL, so sizeof word is 4.
strlen finds three characters before NUL.
Changing element 0 preserves the terminator; %s safely prints bat.

prediction.question: Does the terminator count in strlen(word)?
prediction.answer: No; strlen(word) is 3 while the array capacity is 4.
prediction.explanation: Length excludes NUL; capacity includes space available for it.

lessons.recap: A string needs a reachable NUL; a character array alone is not sufficient.

retrieval.question: Why can strlen not discover the length of an unterminated buffer safely?
retrieval.answer: It searches for NUL without receiving the buffer capacity and may read beyond it.

lessons.title: Make room for the terminator
lessons.objective: Copy and append strings only when destination capacity permits.
explanation: Writing a string needs room for every copied character plus one NUL. A destination with capacity 5 can hold at most four visible characters. The source length and destination capacity are separate facts; neither a pointer nor a string’s contents tells a function the writable capacity.

strcmp compares two valid strings and returns a negative value, zero, or a positive value; test == 0 for equality. strlen measures a valid source. Neither checks destination capacity. Avoid unbounded copying: explicitly verify space or use a carefully specified bounded operation.

Choose and document failure behavior. Our copy exercise creates a terminated prefix when capacity is nonzero and reports truncation. Our append exercise preserves the original destination if the entire suffix will not fit. A bounded result is useful only when the caller knows whether text was lost.
walkthrough: label has capacity 6 but currently stores three characters plus NUL.
extra < capacity - used reserves one element for the terminator.
The loop includes suffix[extra], copying NUL too; label becomes cats.

prediction.question: Would a suffix of length 3 fit after "cat" in label[6]?
prediction.answer: No. Three + three characters + one terminator would need seven elements.
prediction.explanation: The capacity check must account for NUL.

lessons.recap: Bounded text operations specify both capacity and truncation behavior.

retrieval.question: What does strcmp(a, b) == 0 mean?
retrieval.answer: Both valid NUL-terminated strings contain the same byte sequence.

lessons.title: Review bounded data and text
lessons.objective: Apply array bounds and distinguish a safe string from an invalid read.
explanation: Arrays let a function process more than one value, but the function needs a trustworthy count. Write down the invariant: every element read or written has an index less than that count, and the count does not exceed the actual object.

A NUL terminator provides a stopping point for string operations only while it lies inside accessible storage. Safe examples preserve both a capacity bound for writes and a terminator for later reads. Empty datasets and empty strings deserve their own tests.

An out-of-bounds read is undefined behavior. A sample run cannot tell us a portable output, even if it appears to print something plausible. Diagnose the invalid access itself. The following worked example is safe; the diagnosis exercise deliberately presents an invalid read to identify, not to execute for a predicted value.
walkthrough: The caller calculates four elements from the actual array object.
The function reads exactly the count elements using i < count.
Only the two values 8 are greater than 5, so the result is 2.

prediction.question: Should a test of an out-of-bounds read require a specific printed value?
prediction.answer: No. Undefined behavior has no required portable output.
prediction.explanation: The error is the invalid access, not a particular observed result.

lessons.recap: Use count for arrays, capacity plus NUL for strings, and separate empty-case tests.

retrieval.question: What must be true before reading values[i]?
retrieval.answer: The object must still exist, values must refer to it, and i must be inside its valid element range.

lessons.title: An address is a value
lessons.objective: Distinguish a pointer object from the object it designates.
explanation: An object occupies storage during its lifetime. The address-of operator & produces an address for an object. int *p = &value creates a separate pointer object p whose stored value designates the int object value. The star in this declaration is part of the pointer type.

In an expression, *p dereferences a pointer: it accesses the pointed-to object. Assigning *p = 9 changes value, whereas assigning p changes which object p designates. Two pointers can designate the same object; this is aliasing, so a write through one can be observed through the other.

Only dereference a pointer that designates a live object of an appropriate type. NULL, available from <stddef.h>, expresses that a pointer designates no object; it cannot be dereferenced. Actual address numbers vary by run and platform, so our diagram uses symbolic addresses rather than promising one number.
walkthrough: value and p are two different objects: an int and a pointer containing its address.
alias receives the same address; *p = 9 writes to their shared pointed-to object.
Setting p to NULL changes only p; alias still designates the live value object.

prediction.question: After p = NULL, does alias stop designating value?
prediction.answer: No. alias is a separate pointer object and still stores value’s address.
prediction.explanation: Copying an address does not couple later assignments to the pointer objects.

lessons.recap: A pointer object stores an address; dereferencing accesses a different object.

retrieval.question: When is dereferencing a pointer valid?
retrieval.answer: When it designates a live, appropriately typed object at a valid position and the access is permitted.

lessons.title: Return status, write a result
lessons.objective: Use pointer output parameters with a clear success contract.
explanation: A function can return a status and use a pointer parameter for an additional result. int try_half(int input, int *result) can return 1 on success and write *result, or return 0 while leaving the caller’s result unchanged. Document both success and failure behavior.

The caller supplies a live object’s address, and the callee checks NULL if the contract permits it. A NULL check does not prove an arbitrary other address is valid. Pointer types matter: an int * output belongs with an int object, not an unrelated double object.

Use failure checks before writes, so callers can safely retain their earlier values. This helps later input parsers and allocation APIs: a result becomes usable only after status says it succeeded. Pointer parameters themselves remain copies of pointer values; the pointed-to objects are shared.
walkthrough: value starts as an initialized int whose address can safely be passed.
The even argument succeeds, storing 4 and returning status 1.
The odd argument returns before writing, preserving the earlier result 4.

prediction.question: What does the second line print?
prediction.explanation: The failed call leaves the previous successful result unchanged.

lessons.recap: Separate a status from an output value and leave outputs unchanged on failure.

retrieval.question: Why must the caller test status before using an output as a new result?
retrieval.answer: A failed operation may leave it unchanged rather than producing a new valid value.

lessons.title: Arrays are objects, pointers are values
lessons.objective: Use array-to-pointer conversion and bounded pointer arithmetic.
explanation: An array and a pointer are different types of object. In most expressions an array expression converts to a pointer to its first element. It does not convert in sizeof array or &array. A pointer stores an address and carries no array length; sizeof a pointer does not measure the pointed-to array.

A function parameter written int values[] is adjusted to int *values. This explains why array processing functions need an explicit count. With a const int * parameter, the function must not write to the ints through that pointer; const does not mean the pointer itself can never change.

Pointer addition is defined only within one array object and its one-past boundary. A one-past pointer can mark the end but must not be dereferenced. Our examples use count to bound every operation, never compare unrelated objects to infer a length, and never move before the first element.
walkthrough: sizeof values in main observes the real three-element array object.
Passing values converts it to the first element’s address; count travels separately.
current is dereferenced three times within the array; after the final increment it is one-past and never read.

prediction.question: Does the values parameter still know the original array length?
prediction.answer: No; it is a pointer parameter, and count supplies the length separately.
prediction.explanation: Array-to-pointer conversion preserves an address rather than an array-size description.

lessons.recap: Arrays and pointers differ; pointer arithmetic needs one live array and valid bounds.

retrieval.question: May a one-past pointer be dereferenced?
retrieval.answer: No. It can serve as an end marker, but does not designate an element.

lessons.title: Bounds and lifetime travel together
lessons.objective: Review valid pointer operations and identify expired storage.
explanation: For every pointer access, ask two questions: does the designated object still exist, and is the position inside that object’s allowed bounds? A non-NULL value alone answers neither. Keep counts beside array pointers and make ownership or borrowed lifetime explicit in your contract.

Never return the address of an ordinary automatic local object. It ceases to exist when the function exits, so the returned address cannot safely be used to access it. Returning a computed value or borrowing an address from caller-owned live storage avoids that mistake.

Diagrams often label automatic storage “stack” and allocated storage “heap.” Those are useful common implementation models, not a complete description of the ISO C abstract machine. The language guarantees object lifetimes and permitted accesses; it does not require one hardware memory layout.
walkthrough: The caller’s array stays alive throughout the call.
Saving first prevents the first overwrite from losing the value needed at the end.
The early return avoids underflow for count 0; all remaining indices are inside count.

prediction.question: Would returning &first from rotate_left give the caller a usable lasting object?
prediction.answer: No. first’s automatic lifetime ends when the function returns.
prediction.explanation: The array belongs to the caller; first is a different local object with a shorter lifetime.

lessons.recap: A safe address requires a live object and a valid bound, not merely a non-NULL value.

retrieval.question: What do “stack” and “heap” diagrams simplify?
retrieval.answer: Common implementation storage organization; they do not replace C’s object lifetime and access rules.

lessons.title: Read a bounded chunk
lessons.objective: Use fgets while recognizing newline, EOF, and incomplete lines.
explanation: stdin is the standard input stream. In this app it is a supplied text batch, not a live terminal. fgets(buffer, capacity, stdin) reads at most capacity - 1 characters and adds NUL when it succeeds. The supplied capacity must not exceed the actual array size.

fgets keeps a newline if it reads one. strchr, from <string.h>, returns a pointer to a matching character or NULL; use it to find and replace the newline with NUL. A NULL return from fgets means no line was read: inspect ferror for a stream error, otherwise it is EOF.

A successful chunk without newline may be the final line at EOF or the beginning of a longer line. Never assume success means a complete line. This lesson’s exercises explicitly use short lines that fit; the truncation lesson adds a complete-line reader. Unchecked scanf can leave invalid input and conversions unhandled; an unbounded %s can overwrite an array, so we do not use either pattern.
walkthrough: line has sixteen elements, so a successful read stores at most fifteen input characters plus NUL.
If present, the newline is part of the buffer and is replaced through the returned pointer.
Without newline we report only a chunk; a later lesson distinguishes final EOF from truncation.

prediction.question: With stdin set to cat followed by a newline, what is printed?
prediction.explanation: The newline read into line is replaced by NUL before printf supplies its own newline.

lessons.recap: fgets limits a chunk, retains newline, and reports when no input was read.

retrieval.question: Does a successful fgets always read a complete line?
retrieval.answer: No. A long line can be split across calls, and the last line may end at EOF without newline.

lessons.title: A number must consume the intended text
lessons.objective: Validate conversion using the end pointer and errno.
explanation: strtol, declared by <stdlib.h>, converts a base-10 integer to long when called with base 10. It skips initial whitespace and optionally accepts a sign. Its end pointer tells you where conversion stopped. A return value of zero alone cannot distinguish valid 0 from text containing no number.

Set errno to 0 before conversion, then reject end == text (no digits) and errno == ERANGE (not representable as long). Skip trailing whitespace using isspace with an unsigned char cast, then require the end to reach NUL. The cast keeps the character-classification call valid for every byte value.

The numeric exercises include a provided complete-line reader so overlong input is rejected before parsing; its probe-and-drain behavior is unpacked next. Conversion limits are not application limits: after successful conversion, also check the allowed range before storing or calculating.
walkthrough: strtol consumes 42 but leaves x, so the parser rejects the first text.
On failure the output value stays 99; no invalid partial result is stored.
The second input has digits and only surrounding whitespace, so 0 is accepted.

prediction.question: Does strtol returning zero prove that conversion failed?
prediction.answer: No. The text 0 converts successfully to zero.
prediction.explanation: Use the end pointer and errno in addition to the returned value.

lessons.recap: Require digits, a representable long, permitted trailing text, and the application range.

retrieval.question: Why reset errno before calling strtol?
retrieval.answer: A previous call may have left an error; the current conversion needs a fresh check for ERANGE.

lessons.title: Validate the entire line
lessons.objective: Handle EOF and long input without parsing a truncated prefix.
explanation: A destination bound prevents a write overflow, but a truncated prefix can still look like a valid number. If a buffer contains 15 characters without newline, the next input character decides whether the complete line exactly fits, ends at EOF, or is too long.

The provided read_line helper probes with fgetc, which returns int so it can represent any unsigned-char value plus EOF. If the probe is newline or a clean EOF, the buffered text is complete. Otherwise it drains the remainder through newline or EOF and reports too long, preventing the next read from treating the tail as a new line.

Keep stream status, numeric conversion, and application range separate. Reject a truncated line before strtol. After a valid long conversion, check the small application interval before converting to int. An EOF before any input is different from a final complete line without newline; stream errors are a separate outcome.
walkthrough: fgets reserves NUL inside the eight-element array.
The helper uses an int for fgetc and distinguishes EOF from an actual input character.
Only a complete line reaches the parser; the 0..130 range is checked before use.

prediction.question: For stdin 12345678 followed by newline, may the buffered prefix be parsed as an age?
prediction.answer: No. It is rejected as too long before conversion.
prediction.explanation: The program must validate the original complete line, not just a prefix that fits.

lessons.recap: Bounds protect storage; complete-line and range checks protect meaning.

retrieval.question: Why drain a rejected overlong line?
retrieval.answer: So later reads begin at the next line rather than at leftover characters from the rejected input.

lessons.title: Turn input into a checked result
lessons.objective: Compose bounded reading, conversion, and domain validation.
explanation: A robust input path has stages: read a complete line, convert all the intended text, validate the application range, then calculate. Keep rejected input out of the calculation rather than repairing it silently or using an uninitialized value.

Reuse small helpers with explicit status and output contracts. The reader distinguishes EOF, truncation, and stream failure. The parser writes an output only on success. A caller checks those results before using the value, and a quantity or score bound also prevents overflow in later arithmetic.

Test valid boundaries, whitespace, missing input, an extra suffix, and a long line. Tests cover sampled behavior; they do not prove that every input is handled correctly. Explain which errors stop the batch and which permit another line. This checkpoint chooses to stop and print invalid if any required field fails.
walkthrough: Each required field is a complete line read into the bounded buffer.
The parser accepts only the documented quantity and price ranges.
The maximum product is 10,000,000, within the minimum required C long range; only validated values are multiplied.

prediction.question: With lines 3 and 250, what is the result? What if the price is 250x?
prediction.explanation: The trailing x prevents a complete conversion, so multiplication is skipped.

lessons.recap: Compose helpers and calculate only with validated values.

retrieval.question: Why validate a range before arithmetic as well as before a type conversion?
retrieval.answer: The range establishes that later operations are meaningful and representable.

lessons.title: Keep related values together
lessons.objective: Define a struct and read or update its members.
explanation: A struct groups named members into one record. A study session has a duration and a completed flag; keeping them together makes their relationship explicit. Each member still has its own type.

Define the record shape with struct Session. Create an object with that type, initialize every member, and use object.member to read or update it. An initializer without member names follows declaration order.

The -> operator accesses a member through a pointer: p->minutes means (*p).minutes. Check a pointer before dereferencing it when NULL is permitted. Assignment copies a struct value, including its members; it does not create an alias to the original object.
walkthrough: struct Session defines a type; it does not create a session object by itself.
The initializer sets minutes to 25 and done to 0. saved receives a value copy.
Changing today.done affects today. saved.done stays 0 because saved is a separate object.

prediction.question: Does setting today.done also change saved.done?
prediction.explanation: Struct assignment copies member values; these are two distinct objects.

lessons.recap: A record groups members, while . and -> express whether you hold the object or its address.

retrieval.question: How do you access minutes through struct Session *p?
retrieval.answer: p->minutes

lessons.title: Name types and meaningful states
lessons.objective: Use typedef and enum to express a record state without magic numbers.
explanation: A typedef is an additional name for an existing type, not a new object. typedef struct Task Task allows the shorter spelling Task in declarations. Keep names clear enough that readers can tell a record from an ordinary integer.

An enum names a small set of integer constants. Here PENDING and DONE describe states directly. enum does not automatically reject every other integer value; validate externally supplied values before using them.

A switch can handle the named states and have a default branch for an invalid value. Enumerator values need not be contiguous unless your definition makes them so. Compare state names instead of depending on their incidental numbers.
walkthrough: Status is an alias for this enum type; the named constants communicate intent.
Task contains an integer and the named status type.
The switch prints done, and default provides an explicit fallback.

prediction.question: Does typedef allocate a Task object?
prediction.explanation: It creates a type name. The declaration Task task creates the object.

lessons.recap: Names for types and states improve readability, but input validation still matters.

retrieval.question: What does a default switch branch handle here?
retrieval.answer: an unrecognized state

lessons.title: Process a collection of records
lessons.objective: Traverse a bounded record array and derive a result.
explanation: An array of records stores several objects of the same struct type. records[i].minutes selects element i and then its member. The valid index range remains 0 through count - 1; grouping data does not relax bounds.

Pass the array address and its element count separately. A function parameter such as const Task *items does not retain the array length. const here prevents the function from modifying the pointed-to tasks through that pointer.

For an empty collection, count is zero and the loop body does not run. Permit NULL only when count is zero; document that a nonzero count requires that many valid elements. Sum calculations also need range reasoning: our practice totals stay within a documented bound.
walkthrough: sizeof computes the element count here because tasks is an array in this scope.
Each loop iteration examines exactly one record with a valid index.
Only the two completed records contribute, so the output is 25.

prediction.question: Would sizeof items / sizeof items[0] recover count inside a function taking Task *items?
prediction.explanation: items is a pointer parameter. Pass the element count explicitly.

lessons.recap: A record collection still needs explicit length and numeric bounds.

retrieval.question: Which index is the first invalid one in a count-element array?
retrieval.answer: count

lessons.title: Checkpoint: a fixed-capacity record book
lessons.objective: Maintain a bounded collection with clear success and failure outcomes.
explanation: A fixed-capacity collection is a useful first record manager. Keep both capacity and used count. The invariant is 0 <= used <= capacity; elements below used are initialized and the remaining storage is reserved.

Append only when space exists. Validate a record before storing it and increment used after the write succeeds. Deleting shifts later records one position left, then reduces used; the old final slot is outside the active range.

Build the program from small functions for parsing, updating, and displaying. Use a temporary parsed value so bad input cannot partly overwrite existing work. This checkpoint works on supplied records; the project combines it with the validated input functions you already learned.
walkthrough: Three slots exist but only two are initially part of the collection.
The capacity check happens before accessing tasks[used].
The compound literal creates a Task value; post-increment advances used after the index is used.

prediction.question: When used == capacity, may tasks[used] receive an appended record?
prediction.explanation: That index is one past the array, so append must fail without a write.

lessons.recap: Capacity, used count, validation, and failure behavior are the collection contract.

retrieval.question: When should used increase during a successful append?
retrieval.answer: after storing the validated record

lessons.title: Storage sized at runtime
lessons.objective: Allocate initialized storage, check failure, and release it once.
explanation: An automatic local array has a lifetime tied to its enclosing block. Allocated storage instead lasts until you release it with free. Common diagrams call these stack and heap; those names describe typical implementations, not the complete ISO C abstract machine.

malloc returns a suitably aligned address for the requested bytes, or NULL on failure. Its bytes are not initialized. calloc takes an element count and size and initializes the allocated bytes to all-bits-zero; for an int array this represents integer zero.

Compute sizes carefully and check for multiplication overflow before allocating. In C, do not cast malloc: include <stdlib.h> and assign its void pointer result. Check the result before use. Free the allocation once, and stop using all pointers into it after release.
walkthrough: calloc requests three int objects and zero-initializes their representation.
The NULL check runs before any access to values.
The allocation is released after the last read, and no dangling pointer is used.

prediction.question: After free(values), may values[1] be read because the pointer variable still exists?
prediction.explanation: The allocated objects no longer exist. Keeping an address does not extend their lifetime.

lessons.recap: Allocation creates an ownership obligation: check, initialize, use within bounds, and release once.

retrieval.question: Which header declares malloc, calloc, and free?
retrieval.answer: stdlib.h

lessons.title: Make ownership visible
lessons.objective: Document who releases storage and avoid dangling aliases.
explanation: Ownership is a program design rule: one part of the program is responsible for releasing each allocation. C does not enforce that rule. An owning function may transfer the pointer to a caller; a borrowing function uses it temporarily and must not free it.

Copying a pointer copies an address, not its allocation. After the owner frees the allocation, every alias into it becomes unusable. Setting one pointer variable to NULL does not repair other aliases. free(NULL) is permitted, but double-free of the same non-NULL allocation is undefined behavior.

Use a clear failure contract. A copy function either returns a complete independent allocation or NULL; it must not return a partly initialized object. A cleanup function may reset the owner pointer after release so repeated cleanup through that same owner variable is harmless.
walkthrough: owner is responsible for freeing the allocation; borrowed refers to the same int.
The only dereference occurs while that int is alive.
Setting owner to NULL documents cleanup but borrowed still contains a dangling address.

prediction.question: Does owner = NULL make borrowed point to a live object again?
prediction.explanation: Pointer assignment affects one variable; it does not recreate an allocation or update aliases.

lessons.recap: Distinguish ownership transfer from borrowing and remember that free invalidates all aliases.

retrieval.question: What is wrong with freeing both owner and borrowed when they share one allocation?
retrieval.answer: double free

lessons.title: Grow without losing the old allocation
lessons.objective: Use realloc with checked size arithmetic and an atomic failure contract.
explanation: realloc may move an allocation. On success, the old pointer and all aliases into it must stop being used; use the returned pointer. On failure for a nonzero size, it returns NULL and the original allocation remains valid.

Never write owner = realloc(owner, bytes) directly when you need to preserve ownership on failure. Store the result in a temporary pointer, then commit it only on success. New bytes are uninitialized, so a growing container must initialize newly active elements before reading them.

Keep separate length and capacity. Grow only when length reaches capacity, guard both doubling and element-size multiplication, and allow growth failure without changing length, capacity, or the owner. This is a transactional update pattern applied to memory.
walkthrough: grown preserves the original owner until realloc succeeds.
After success, items receives the new address; the earlier address must not be used.
The new elements are initialized before being read, and the current allocation is freed once.

prediction.question: On realloc failure for a nonzero request, has the original allocation been freed?
prediction.explanation: The caller retains the original allocation and must eventually free it.

lessons.recap: Check arithmetic, use a temporary pointer, and commit owner/capacity only after success.

retrieval.question: Why is assigning realloc directly to the sole owning pointer dangerous?
retrieval.answer: it loses the original pointer on failure

lessons.title: Checkpoint: ownership under pressure
lessons.objective: Review allocation failures and verify a small owned collection.
explanation: An allocation audit follows each owner from creation to release. List success, early return, invalid-input, and allocation-failure paths. Every successful allocation needs exactly one eventual release, and every borrowed address must stop being used before the object lifetime ends.

When copying a collection, allocate a new buffer and copy only initialized elements. Handle the empty case explicitly. Failure should leave the source unchanged and should not leak a partially built destination.

Tests can reveal bad bounds or cleanup, but passing tests does not prove lifetime safety. Later sanitizer lessons help detect certain mistakes. Keep contracts, manual ownership reasoning, and runtime checking together rather than relying on any one of them.
walkthrough: sizeof source is the whole fixed array byte count in this scope.
The new allocation receives independent initialized values.
Changing the source does not affect the copy, which is released after use.

prediction.question: Does copying the pointer itself create independent elements?
prediction.explanation: A pointer copy aliases the same allocation. Independent storage requires allocation and element copying.

lessons.recap: Follow every owner across success and failure; copy values into new storage when independence is required.

retrieval.question: Who frees a successful allocation returned by an ownership-transferring function?
retrieval.answer: the caller

lessons.title: Save text and check every I/O stage
lessons.objective: Open, write, read, and close a text file with explicit error handling.
explanation: FILE is the standard library’s stream type. fopen(path, "r") opens an existing text file for reading; "w" creates or truncates a file for writing. Failure returns NULL, so check before using the stream. Never overwrite an important file casually: "w" discards its previous contents.

Output can fail after opening, and even fclose can report a buffered-write failure. Check fprintf or fputs and the close result. A successful open alone does not mean the data was saved. A useful application reports failure to the user instead of claiming success.

fgets returns NULL for both end-of-file and a read error. After a read loop, ferror distinguishes an error from ordinary EOF. Use a documented text format and validation when loading: persistent bytes are input, so malformed files must not become partially trusted state.
walkthrough: The program creates a disposable teaching file; w mode intentionally truncates it.
ok records write success and is also cleared if closing reports an error.
The file is reopened for reading and every opened stream is eventually closed.

prediction.question: Can fclose report a write error even when fprintf previously succeeded?
prediction.explanation: Buffered output may reach the underlying file later; close must be checked.

lessons.recap: Saving has multiple failure stages, and loading persisted text requires the same validation as other input.

retrieval.question: What distinguishes a read error from ordinary EOF after fgets returns NULL?
retrieval.answer: ferror

lessons.title: A command line is input too
lessons.objective: Validate command-line arguments and document an interoperable text format.
explanation: int main(int argc, char *argv[]) receives a count and an array of argument strings. argc includes the program name; argv[1] is the first user argument only when argc > 1. These are strings, so a number still needs parsing and range checks.

Define a tiny format before saving records. For example, one nonnegative duration per line, decimal digits only, no extra fields, and a stated maximum count. Decide whether blank lines and leading spaces are permitted. The reader and writer must implement the same rules.

Error output belongs on stderr and usage information should tell the user how to recover. A nonzero return status signals failure to scripts. Do not concatenate arguments into shell commands; open the filename directly with library calls.
walkthrough: argc is checked before argv[1] is read.
strtol supplies the stopping address and reports a range error through errno.
The application applies its own 0..600 bound after conversion.

prediction.question: For a command launched as minutes 25, how many arguments does argc normally count?
prediction.explanation: The program name and the supplied number are separate argument strings.

lessons.recap: Arguments and files are external input: validate shape, conversion, range, and failure status.

retrieval.question: Why must argc be checked before reading argv[1]?

lessons.title: One program, several source files
lessons.objective: Separate declarations from definitions and link a multi-file program.
explanation: A declaration tells the compiler the name and type of something; a definition supplies a function body or storage. Put public function declarations in a .h header and each ordinary function definition in one .c file. Include your own header in both callers and implementations so disagreement is caught early.

The compiler translates each .c file separately. The linker then connects calls to definitions. A missing definition is a linking problem, different from a syntax error during compilation. Do not include one .c file inside another as a substitute for the normal build process.

Include guards prevent a header’s contents from being processed repeatedly within one translation unit. A guard uses #ifndef, #define, and #endif around the declarations. A Makefile expresses build dependencies; changes to a header should rebuild every object that relies on it.

The definition supplies the body; the worked version keeps it in one file only to show the distinction.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: a reproducible CLI build
lessons.objective: Combine file contracts, error paths, modules, and an explicit build command.
explanation: A reproducible build states the language standard and useful warnings rather than inheriting compiler defaults. This course uses C17: -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic. Warnings are evidence to investigate, not a reason to turn every beginner warning into an error.

A small Makefile can compile .c files into .o files and link an executable, with headers as dependencies. A target recipe starts with a tab. Use clean to remove generated files; keep source files and saved learner data out of that removal list.

The final program needs a contract for argument handling, file syntax, range limits, and ownership. Test both successful data and failure paths. During development, build with -g and a low optimization level; diagnostic sanitizer builds come next and require suitable runner support.

-std=c17 selects the intended C dialect and warnings remain enabled.
-g prepares useful source information for a debugger.

lessons.title: Investigate before changing code
lessons.objective: Use compiler warnings and a repeatable debugger workflow.
explanation: Begin debugging by writing the expected behavior, a small reproducing input, and the actual result. Rebuild with -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -g -O0. Fix the first relevant diagnostic before assuming later messages are independent problems.

GDB can stop at a source line and inspect a live program. A basic session uses break main, run, next, print variable, and continue. next steps over a function call; step enters it. A debugger observation applies to that execution, not every possible input.

For a logic bug, trace one variable and check the loop’s boundaries. For a crash, inspect the call backtrace and object lifetime. Compiler diagnostics, debugger state, and test results answer different questions; preserve the original evidence rather than guessing at a cause.

lessons.title: Let runtime tools test your hypotheses
lessons.objective: Use ASan and UBSan while understanding what they do not prove.
explanation: AddressSanitizer can detect many out-of-bounds accesses and use-after-free errors in executions it observes. UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer can detect selected undefined operations, such as some invalid shifts and signed overflow. Neither finds every C error or proves a program correct.

A diagnostic build commonly uses -fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-omit-frame-pointer -g with a supported GCC or Clang toolchain. These runtimes need extra memory and virtual-address space, so the isolated runner must use tested limits rather than an arbitrary tight address-space cap.

When a sanitizer reports an error, inspect the first relevant source frame and allocation or release history. Reproduce with the smallest input, fix the underlying bounds or lifetime rule, and run the failing case plus ordinary cases again. Do not merely suppress the diagnostic or demand an output from undefined behavior.
walkthrough: Only indices 0 and 1 belong to this allocation.
The read happens before free; both accessed elements have been initialized.
A clean run gives evidence about this path but does not prove all uses of similar code safe.

prediction.question: Does a clean ASan run prove the program has no lifetime bug on any input?
prediction.explanation: Only executed paths and the sanitizer’s supported checks are observed.

lessons.recap: Tools help catch specific errors; contracts, bounds, and ownership reasoning remain necessary.

lessons.title: Know what the language promises
lessons.objective: Distinguish undefined, unspecified, and implementation-defined behavior.
explanation: Undefined behavior means the language imposes no requirements for that execution. Examples include signed integer overflow and reading through a dangling pointer. Do not collect a sample output and teach it as the answer.

Unspecified behavior permits several possibilities without requiring the implementation to document which one it chooses; function-argument evaluation order is a common example when the operations themselves are valid. Implementation-defined behavior requires a documented choice, such as whether plain char has the range of signed char or unsigned char.

C17 is this course’s deliberate baseline, not the latest C standard. C23 adds features and changes some rules; use them only in a separately labeled context with a compiler that supports them. Type widths can vary, so use limits headers and appropriate types rather than assuming 32-bit int or signed overflow wrapping.
walkthrough: <limits.h> describes the current implementation’s integer ranges.
The output is deliberately implementation-dependent; neither one fixed int width nor char signedness is promised.
No overflowing arithmetic is performed to discover the range.

prediction.question: Is signed integer overflow guaranteed to wrap in C17?
prediction.explanation: Signed overflow is undefined behavior. Unsigned arithmetic has different, modulo rules.

lessons.recap: Classify the rule before predicting output, and consult implementation limits for portable code.

retrieval.question: Which category requires the implementation to document its choice?
retrieval.answer: implementation-defined

lessons.title: Checkpoint: evidence for a release
lessons.objective: Combine independent cases, bounds reasoning, and diagnostic tools.
explanation: A release check starts from each function contract. Include ordinary input, empty input, boundaries, malformed data, resource failure, and repeated operations. Tests should check observable behavior across those categories, not require a single textual implementation.

Keep runner failures distinct from learner failures. A compilation error is different from a failed assertion, a runtime crash, a timeout, or infrastructure unavailable. If a tool is unavailable, say so; never replace a missing execution with a simulated passing result.

The final tracker project combines initialized records, dynamic ownership, validated input, file persistence, and a multi-file build. Inspect one complete record through create, update, save, reload, and free. Passing the rubric demonstrates those tested skills; it does not guarantee all C programs are safe.
walkthrough: The input list covers below-bound, exact low, middle, exact high, and above-bound cases.
The function contract assumes low <= high and makes no unsafe arithmetic.
These five cases support this small contract; they do not test every function or resource failure.

prediction.question: Why test both the exact bound and just outside it?
prediction.explanation: Incorrect < versus <= logic can treat the exact bound differently from the adjacent case.

lessons.recap: Use distinct edge categories, preserve evidence, and report exactly what was verified.

retrieval.question: Does a passing sanitizer-and-test suite prove a program correct?
retrieval.answer: no
